section_summary: This section consists chiefly of Spanish-language articles from Mexican periodicals presenting favorable interpretations of Japanese society, culture, economic policy, imperial loyalty, naval policy and industrial development during 1934-1936. Several articles defend Japanese policy in North China and Manchukuo while portraying the Soviet Union and Soviet influence in Mongolia as threats to peace in East Asia. The section begins with the conclusion of a story about two girls named Nobuko at the Japanese landing-force headquarters in Shanghai and ends partway through an article on Soviet-Japanese relations.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of article on the two Nobuko, the “flowers of the battlefield”
subfiles.from: La Fragancia de la Flor del Cerezo
subfiles.about: The conclusion recounts the conduct of two girls named Nobuko at the Japanese landing-force headquarters during fighting in Shanghai.
subfiles.summary: Article excerpt on two girls called the 'flowers of the battlefield' who prepare soup for Rear Admiral Uematsu's command and say they would rather die beside him; he intends to seek official recognition.

subfiles.title: El Japón y el Tratado de Wáshington
subfiles.about: The article defends Japan's planned denunciation of the Washington Naval Treaty and demands naval parity.
subfiles.summary: It argues that the 5:5:3 naval ratio imposed on the United States, Britain and Japan reflected temporary conditions in 1921 rather than enduring defense requirements. Longer-range ships and aircraft, the transformation of Hawaii into an advanced base, Soviet military growth in East Asia and the restrictions of the 1930 London treaty are presented as reasons Japan can no longer accept inferiority. Japan proposes equal naval rights, genuine arms reduction and a reduction of offensive forces, summarized as replacing 5:5:3 with 2:2:2.

subfiles.title: La Mujer Japonesa
subfiles.about: The article describes the character, domestic position, historical prominence and legal status of Japanese women.
subfiles.summary: Japanese women are portrayed as gentle in appearance but exceptionally courageous, industrious and resilient, with the middle-class wife presented as the foundation of household and empire. Historical examples range from Empress Jingū and Murasaki Shikibu to Masako, while the article traces women's status through the Nara, Heian, Kamakura and Tokugawa periods. It acknowledges women's lack of voting and electoral rights but describes intellectual progress and an active suffrage movement.

subfiles.title: Al Margen de la Caricatura del “Vanity Fair”
subfiles.about: The article explains Japanese outrage over a Vanity Fair caricature of the Emperor of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mexican article on the Vanity Fair caricature: insulting and the cause of a protest; the emperor is sacred to Japanese, citing Nogi and Togo; foreign publications must respect Japanese sentiment.

subfiles.title: Las Corrientes Intelectuales en el Japón
subfiles.about: The article surveys Japanese intellectual adaptability, mass publishing and efforts to simplify written Japanese.
subfiles.summary: It attributes Japan's development to a combination of receptivity, assimilation, harmony and a preference for practical action. Large newspaper and magazine circulations, high literacy and several popular books are offered as evidence of a vigorous reading culture. The article describes a shift from foreign translations toward renewed study of Japanese culture and advocates reducing the number of Chinese characters used in print to make literacy and foreign study of Japanese easier.

subfiles.title: El Movimiento Autónomo de la China del Norte
subfiles.about: The article denies that Japan created the North China autonomy movement and presents it as a spontaneous Chinese reaction to Nanjing rule.
subfiles.summary: Article on North China's autonomy movement: regional divisions weaken Nanjing, taxation and silver nationalization cause discontent; Japan denies a partition policy but cites Manchukuo's security and Tanggu Truce rights.

subfiles.title: La Literatura Japonesa Contemporánea
subfiles.from: Kan Kikuchi; reprinted in El Universal
subfiles.about: Kikuchi Kan surveys the foreign influences, literary schools and distinctive forms of contemporary Japanese literature.
subfiles.summary: Japan's literary world is described as a melting pot of Russian, northern European, German, Austrian, French, British, American and indigenous traditions. The article traces realism, the humanitarian Shirakaba school, the New Technique school and the rise and decline of proletarian literature. It identifies the introspective “personal novel” as a distinctively Japanese form and argues that linguistic subtleties make Japanese literature exceptionally difficult to translate for Western readers.

subfiles.title: “Dar y Tomar”, el Principio que Guía al Comercio Japonés
subfiles.about: The article defends Japanese trade policy as reciprocal and peaceful while surveying protectionism and economic blocs worldwide.
subfiles.summary: Japan is said to favor unconditional most-favored-nation treatment but to require defensive trade legislation against discriminatory foreign measures. The article surveys currency depreciation, import restrictions, tariff wars, imperial preference and regional economic blocs in Europe and the Americas. Japanese trade figures for 1934 are used to argue that Japan imported more than it exported and that its commercial growth reflected efficiency, low costs and technical improvement rather than unfair aggression.

subfiles.title: La Mujer Japonesa Frente a un Aspecto Nuevo de la Vida
subfiles.about: The article describes the displacement of women's cultural emancipation by nationalism and economic regeneration in 1930s Japan.
subfiles.summary: It argues that the internationalist movement for women's emancipation, liberal marriage and suffrage declined after the 1931 Sino-Japanese conflict as national duty took precedence over individual freedom. “Bride schools” promoted domestic virtues, while rural women assumed practical responsibilities for debt reduction, temperance, household economy and local rehabilitation. Despite this conservative shift, urban women continued seeking education and paid work, and schoolgirls identified serenity and health as their ideals.

subfiles.title: Elementos Espirituales en la Industria Japonesa
subfiles.about: The article attributes Japan's industrial success to a long-standing spiritual ethic of craftsmanship as well as modern technical learning.
subfiles.summary: It rejects the idea that Japanese industry arose solely from recent imitation of Europe and America, emphasizing centuries of artistic precision, devotion and Bushidō-influenced discipline. The story of swordsmith Yoshihiro submitting to Masamune illustrates the claim that technical skill requires spiritual dedication. The same ethic is credited with the success of modern textile factories and is joined to a call for mutual concession in international commerce.

subfiles.title: El Problema del Extremo Oriente
subfiles.about: The article portrays Soviet border actions and communist expansion as the central threat to Manchukuo and East Asia.
subfiles.summary: It recounts a March clash at Changlingzi in which Soviet border troops allegedly attacked Japanese personnel from Manchukuo and then fired upon reinforcements from Hunchun. Soviet policy is depicted as a continuation of Russian imperial expansion through Siberia, Outer Mongolia, Xinjiang and Shanxi. The article contends that Soviet military preparations and French support have created the conditions for more aggressive action in the Far East.

subfiles.title: El Espíritu Militar Japonés
subfiles.about: The article interprets the February 26 Incident as proof of the Japanese military's overriding obedience to the emperor.
subfiles.summary: Article on Japanese military spirit: young officers resisted until an imperial order sent them back, showing no Japanese can oppose the emperor's will; suicide stories dramatize loyalty versus duty.

subfiles.title: El Modernismo en el Japón
subfiles.about: The article examines Japan's adaptation of Chinese and Western culture and the resulting character of Japanese modernism.
subfiles.summary: It argues that Japanese culture began with continental influences but transformed imported institutions, arts and ideas through sustained adaptation. Dutch learning at Edo and Nagasaki, vernacular literature, Hōryū-ji and Yōmeimon illustrate the complicated relationship between foreign models and Japanese identity. Modern Western fashions in literature, architecture, philosophy, music and entertainment are said to arrive rapidly and often disappear rapidly, yet the author expects Japan eventually to contribute a vigorous culture of its own.

subfiles.title: El Soviet y el Japón
subfiles.about: The article analyzes Soviet-Japanese relations through Soviet support for Outer Mongolia and the 1936 Soviet-Mongolian mutual-assistance pact.
subfiles.summary: Article on Soviet-Japanese relations since 1925 in three stages ending in Manchukuo-Outer Mongolia border conflict, Moscow's concealed control of Mongolia, the failed Manzhouli conference and a mutual-assistance pact; continues beyond this section.
